prompt: You move from 5 cm to 20 cm away from a point charge, four times further out. What happens to the POTENTIAL?

options.text: It falls to a quarter, because V = kQ/r has a plain r
It falls to a sixteenth, because of the inverse square
It is unchanged, because potential is a scalar

explanation: A quarter. The potential carries a plain r, so four times the distance means a quarter of the value. Only the FIELD is squared. Test 1 question 4 confirms it: 720 kV at 5 cm becomes 180 kV at 20 cm, exactly a quarter. Had you squared it you would have looked for a sixteenth and found no such option.

why.a: Correct, and the printed answers on the paper confirm the quarter.
why.b: Wrong. A sixteenth is what the FIELD would do, not the potential.
why.c: Wrong. Being a scalar means it has no direction, not that it ignores distance.
why.d: Wrong direction: moving away lowers the potential.
why.e: Wrong. A half would need r to appear as a square root.

prompt: The potential energy of a charge q sitting at a potential V is U = qV, measured in {{1}}.
explanation: Joules. Coulombs times volts gives joules, because a volt is defined as a joule per coulomb. That is also why W = qV computes a work in joules from a charge and a voltage.

prompt: The work done moving a charge through a potential difference is W = qV, charge times voltage.
explanation: True, and it is simply the definition of potential difference turned around: a volt IS a joule per coulomb, so multiplying coulombs by volts returns joules. It is the reason no work is done along an equipotential, where V does not change at all.

why.true: Correct. Charge times voltage gives energy.
why.false: Wrong. It follows directly from the definition of the volt as a joule per coulomb.

prompt: A uniform field exists between two parallel plates 2 mm apart with 60 V across them. What is the field strength?
explanation: Convert first: 2 mm = 0.002 m. Then E = V/d = 60 / 0.002 = 30000 V/m. Note the size: a modest 60 V across a very small gap gives an enormous field, which is exactly why capacitors are built with plates close together and why they eventually break down.

why.b: Wrong by a factor of 1000, from leaving the gap in millimetres.
why.c: Wrong. This multiplies rather than divides.
why.d: Wrong, and upside down: 0.002 divided by 60.
why.e: Wrong by a factor of ten in the conversion.

prompt: An equipotential is a surface on which the potential is the same everywhere, so moving a charge along it does {{1}} work.
explanation: No work at all. W = qV depends on the CHANGE in potential, and along an equipotential there is none. Field lines always cross such a surface at right angles, because any component along it would create a potential difference and contradict the definition.
